lesson.title: Negating the Pronoun
lesson.subtitle: Placing no right before the walking pronoun: no lo quiero, no la quiero

hook.title: The Shield in Front of the Pronoun
hook.content: When an object pronoun walks in front of the verb (lo quiero, la comprendo), where does no go? It steps in front of the whole pronoun+verb unit: No lo quiero ('I don't want it'), No lo comprendo ('I don't understand it').

pattern.title: Two Ways to Negate with an Infinitive
pattern.content: When an infinitive is present, the pronoun can either hook onto the tail of the infinitive (No quiero confirmarlo) OR walk to the front before quiero (No lo quiero confirmar) — and in both cases, no stands at the very front!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: no lo quiero, no la quiero, no lo comprendo, comprar, ver
exercises.meaning: I don't want it (masculine), I don't want it (feminine), I don't understand it, to buy, to see
exercises.explanation: no always leads the entire pronoun + verb block.

exercises.prompt: Hook 'lo' ('it') onto the tail of 'comprar' ('to buy') to form 'to buy it':
exercises.explanation: comprar + lo welds into one word: comprarlo.

exercises.idea: say you don't want it (referring to the masculine coffee)
cues: masculine 'it' walks before quiero: lo quiero
exercises.explanation: No lo quiero — no shields the front of the lo quiero block.

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'No la quiero'?
exercises.meaning: I don't want it (feminine) (literal Spanish blueprint: Not it (feminine) I-want)
exercises.explanation: No stands before la, which stands before quiero.

summary.outcome: Position 'no' before walking object pronouns and negated infinitives.

use_example.german: No la quiero — no quiero comprarla hoy.
use_example.english: I don't want it — I don't want to buy it today.

summary.takeaway: Pronoun and conjugated verb form an inseparable block — no stands guard in front of both.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([5] Ser & Estar: The Two Beings): discover why Spanish sees 'to be' through two different lenses.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'I don't want to confirm it'
twist.explanation: With the infinitive, lo hooks onto the tail: No quiero confirmarlo.

no.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn → Spanish no. Negation in Spanish is beautifully direct: place no right before the verb cluster.

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

la.etymology_derivation: Latin illa → la. It functions as both the feminine definite article ('the') and the direct object pronoun ('her / it').

confirmar.etymology_derivation: confirmación → confirmar. Strip -ación, attach -ar. One rule turns hundreds of nouns into verbs.

organizar.context_translation: I want to organize the party.
organizar.etymology_derivation: organización → organizar. The infinitive in -ar is stressed on the final syllable.

ver.context_translation: I am going to see it/him today.
ver.etymology_derivation: Pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive: verlo ('to see it/him')!

comprar.etymology_derivation: Latin comparāre ('to get ready, purchase') — English compare.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).
